chunks: "Usually it's the source and the body. On basically every discrete MOSFET they're shorted together inside the package, which is why you only see three pins. There are two reasons.
First, the body forms a PN junction with the source and another with the drain, and those have to stay reverse-biased or at zero.
Tying the body to the source guarantees the source-body junction can never forward-bias. Second, it kills the body effect.
The threshold voltage depends on the source-to-body voltage: if the source rises above the body, the depletion region under the gate widens, the gate has to support more charge, and V t goes up.
Tie them together, V SB is zero, and V t stays at its nominal value. The side effect is the body diode.
Once the body is on the source, the body-drain junction becomes a diode from source to drain in an NFET, so a single MOSFET only blocks voltage in one direction.
That's why battery protection circuits use two FETs back to back. In ICs it's different.
All the NMOS transistors usually share the P-substrate tied to ground, so a stacked NFET can't have its body on its source, and you just design around the body effect.
The other pair people tie is gate and drain, which makes a diode-connected transistor for current mirrors."
